A passage between statements of the main theme that uses fragments and sequences to change key; found in fugues, rondos and concertos.
Italian “narrow”: close imitation in which a fugue subject enters again before the previous statement has finished.
Italian “little return”: the orchestral refrain of a Baroque concerto, returning between solo episodes, often in related keys and in pieces.
A set of continuous variations over a repeating bass or harmonic pattern, usually in slow triple time.
Variations over a short repeating bass or chord pattern in triple time, close kin to the passacaglia; a Spanish dance made serious.
Italian “joke”: a fast movement in triple time, usually with a slower trio, that replaced the minuet in symphonies and quartets.
The dance movement of Classical symphonies and quartets: a minuet in three beats, a contrasting trio, then the minuet again.
Italian “touched”: a keyboard showpiece in fast, even running notes that tests the player’s hands.
A piece that follows the player’s imagination rather than a set form, with sudden changes of speed, texture and key.
A piece that precedes another, or an independent short piece without a set form, often built on one figure or texture.
A short, lyrical piano piece with a singing melody over a broken-chord accompaniment, a form the Irish composer John Field made popular.
German art song for solo voice and piano, setting a poem with equal care for words and accompaniment.
A self-contained song for one voice in an opera, oratorio or cantata, where the action pauses for a character’s feeling.
Sung speech: a vocal line that follows the rhythm and pitch of the words, used between arias to carry the story.
A single-movement orchestral work that tells a story or paints a subject, with its form shaped by the programme.
Instrumental music tied to a story, picture or poem that the composer published or implied.
